content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers challenges that arise in the multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach to traffic signal control, in particular where there are multiple intersections and each intersection is controlled by an agent that can only observe its own intersection. It aims to address two challenges. First, to reduce the need for interacting with the environment in order to learn the system dynamics. Second, to find policies that are fair, where fairness means that each intersection has similar traffic congestion. It proposes a Dyna-style technique for sampling historical trajectories in order to reduce the need for obtaining new observations via environment interaction. To improve on the second challenge, it adds a regularization term to the reward function that penalizes when an intersection has a much lower rate of congestion than the system mean.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper is well written and has a strong motive – it's clear after reading the introduction that this is a problem worth solving and it is easy to interpret why the proposed solutions are effective at mitigating the two challenges. The authors position their approach well with respect to other works in MARL traffic control, and the experiments provide several state-of-the-art techniques as benchmarks.

Turning to weaknesses, fairness in machine learning has been studied extensively, but this paper does not position its notion of fairness with respect to other fairness literature. In fact, although fairness is frequently quoted in this paper, I'd actually characterize this paper not as one of fairness, but as a more global perspective to improving traffic congestion. If fairness is kept as the framework there are important positioning questions to ask. E.g. is this improving group fairness or individual fairness? Are we considering each intersection as an "individual" or are the vehicles themselves the "individuals"? The following paper provides a broad framing for fairness in ML and would be a good starting point for fairness taxonomy: Chouldechova, Alexandra, and Aaron Roth. "The frontiers of fairness in machine learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.08810 (2018).

While individually the two contributions make sense, it is not clear why they are being included together in the same paper. I can guess as to why they are intertwined – I suspect that the proposed fairness model necessitates a learning approach that is optimized for sampling efficiency because the reward signal is constructed based on the unobserved portion of agent state, which means that it will take more observations for the agent to learn. However, I am uncertain if this is the case since there is not much discussion for how these two challenges are related.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Section 4.2, paragraphs two and three in particular, glosses over some extremely dense technical topics without pause for voiceover or problem framing. E.g. I am unable to understand the significance of this sentence without any other context: "To further alleviate model bias and reduce the gap between the performance of MBRL and MFRL, this work incorporates aleatoric uncertainty into MBRL via probabilistic networks and captures epistemic uncertainty by learning an ensemble of dynamics models Chua et al. (2018)." I encourage more discussion that grounds the technical aspects back to the real-world aspects of traffic congestion.

Miscellaneous Comments and Minor Suggestions
--------------------------------------------
Section 4.3 – I know that the agent receives rewards that consider the other intersections, but how is an agent going to learn this if it never observes anything other than its local intersection? I encourage the authors to consider adding in text that provides intuition for how this is possible.

Figure 2 – does the increase in queue length at ~32 episodes indicate the instability of FMA2C? If so, this seems like a fairly major issue worth addressing.

Figure 3 – the CV and Min Queue portions of plots (c) and (d) are too small to be discernible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problems identified in this paper are worth solving and relate to fairness in machine learning. However, this paper seems to be two minor contributions packaged together as one major contribution. I think that the more support is needed for why these two problems, and therefore solutions, are connected. I also think that this paper needs to provide more references and positioning for how it relates to the broader community of fairness in machine learning. Finally, I encourage the inclusion of more analysis on the proposed approach. E.g. the impact of varying the regularization weight in the fairness reward. Overall, I think this paper needs more work before being accepted.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The work proposes a model-based multi-agent reinforcement learning method for traffic signal control with improved fairness metrics via a reward design that accounts for fairness. By modeling the multi-intersection traffic signal control problem as a multi-agent reinforcement learning problem, the method combines ensemble model with model-based reinforcement learning to improve data efficiency. Experiments on comparative study show that the method has comparable or better performance over other MFRL methods. In terms of fairness metric, the proposed method is also better.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
strength: the work achieves a good performance on traffic signal control with good data efficiency and fairness. The method itself is easy to understand and the reward design makes sense to improve fairness among different intersections.

weakness: the algorithm itself does not have much novelty and the results and experiment section is not presented with high quality. It is commonly recognized that model-based reinforcement learning is more data efficient. Also, though this particular design of reward is not presented for traffic signal control, the similar spirit of fairness reward design has been applied to other field. The author claimed that they are the first to take fairness into account for the multi-intersection traffic signal control, which is not true. The paper "Li, Duowei, Jianping Wu, Ming Xu, Ziheng Wang, and Kezhen Hu. "Adaptive traffic signal control model on intersections based on deep reinforcement learning." Journal of Advanced Transportation 2020 (2020)." already did something similar though they did not explicitly mention to improve fairness but the improvement of queue length and/or queue time is equivalent to what the authors are looking to improve in this work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the method is presented with enough clarity, and the algorithm description is clear. However, figure 2 has tiny fonts and the methods' name can hardly be recognizable. It is also not clear in table 1 why for the same task, multiple results from multiple methods are highlighted (e.g. Ing. Single task, IDQN/IPPO/FM2Light are all highlighted). It seems the proposed method not always perform the best among all the tasks, but it is not clear the reason for that. 

Quality and Novelty: the paper's novelty is limited, since it is well known that model-based reinforcement learning is data efficient, and using ensemble method to learn dynamics model is also used in previous papers. (Kurtland Chua, Roberto Calandra, Rowan McAllister, and Sergey Levine. Deep reinforcement learn- ing in a handful of trials using probabilistic dynamics models. Advances in neural information processing systems, 31, 2018.). But the experiments are of relatively high quality since the task is relatively challenging.

Reproducibility: there is no code for this work available. On the other hand, the paper itself also did not provide enough implementation details, so the reproducibility is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall speaking, the work is of high quality in terms of the task and performance, but the used method is of limited novelty. The presentation of the figures and results could be improved. The authors claim they are the first  to take fairness into account for the multi-intersection traffic signal control, which is not true. Therefore, the contribution part should be improved.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Fairness and sample deficiency are two major concerns in this paper, and the authors propose a model to handle these concerns in traffic light control problem. The writing and demonstration of this paper are good, and the experiments and results seem solid and convincing. My main concern is that this paper seems to be just a stack of various existed methods, such as IDQN, model-based RL, coefficient of variation.

- The citation format is chaotic: some have parenthesis while some don’t
- Fairness issues should be reviewed in the related work since it is the main contribution of this work
- More details and introduction about traffic signal control since main readers are from cs community and they may not know traffic control quite well

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes FM2Light, a model-based MARL framework which takes into account the fairness among the intersections (agents) via an additional reward term.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- The problem of traffic intersection control is well motivated and the potential benefits of using MARL is clear. It is intuitively appealing to formulate the control of multiple intersections as a multi-agent problem so that optimizing for one intersection does not negatively affect traffic in the adjacent ones.
- The experiments are set up nicely in a realistic scenario, and comprehensive in terms of baselines, seeds, etc. 

Weakness
1. Concerns regarding IDQN 

- Independent deep Q-network (IDQN) is used as the optimization method, and this is not a principled approach, especially if the goal is to maximize both efficiency and fairness among the multiple agents. 

- Essentially, each agent in IDQN is treating the other agents as stationary and the Q-network is now just an individual utility function which does not satisfy the Bellman equations. 

- Unless I am missing something, the fairness reward is not enough to combat the non-stationarity during training induced by IDQN.

2. Similarly, the dynamics model only conditions on individual actions, and is thus not consistent with the underlying dynamics in the Multi-Agent MDP which should condition on joint actions.
3. The results shown in Figure 3 don’t seem to show much difference between adding or not the fairness reward to FM2Light. Thus, it is unclear how important the fairness reward is. 
4. The problem setting is ambiguous. If each agent is optimizing $r_t^i = -p_t^i$, then wouldn’t the problem become non-cooperative (unless the ultimate goal is to maximize the sum of all individual rewards)? 
5. If the setting is cooperative, the MDP formulation should be a Multi-Agent MDP (MMDP) [1] as the action space is factorized into multiple agents, and each agent can observe the full state (or Dec-POMDP if it is partially observable).


[1] Frans A. Oliehoek and Christopher Amato. 2016. A Concise Introduction to Decentralized POMDPs (1st. ed.). Springer Publishing Company, Incorporated.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: While the problem itself (traffic signal control) is well-motivated and intuitively appealing to formulate as a multi-agent problem, there are many parts of the paper which are not principled from the MARL perspective. The algorithm itself is also a combination of pre-existing approaches and lacks novelty in terms of approach or insight.
content.summary_of_the_review: There are a number of concerns regarding the formulation of the problem (e.g. different reward functions for each agent) as well as the approach (both IDQN and the dynamics model). Furthermore, the experimental results only show minimal improvements at best in terms of performance compared to baselines. Thus, I recommend rejection for the paper at this time.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments. 

The dynamics models in the ensemble are all conditioned on joint action and state. Each dynamics model can be represented as: 
$p_{\phi_{j}}=\operatorname{Pr}\left(\boldsymbol{s}\_{t+1},  \boldsymbol{\hat{r}}\_{t+1} \mid \boldsymbol{s}\_{t}, \boldsymbol{a}\_{t}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}\_{\phi_{j}}\left(\boldsymbol{s}\_{t}, \boldsymbol{a}\_{t}\right), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\_{\phi\_{j}}\left(\boldsymbol{s}\_{t}, \boldsymbol{a}\_{t}\right)\right)$, where $\boldsymbol{s}\_{t}$, $\boldsymbol{a}\_{t}$ and $\boldsymbol{\hat{r}}\_{t+1}$ are joint state, action, and reward, which has been stated in Section 4.2.

As stated in Section 5.2, our FM2Light outperforms all other baselines on all multi-intersection control tasks on both fairness dimensions, yielding average improvements of 11.8% and 19.4% over the best baseline with respect to |CV| and Max Queue, respectively. The results demonstrate the importance of the proposed fairness-aware reward.

For IDQN, the ultimate goal is to maximize the sum of all individual rewards. Our proposed fairness-aware reward function well balances the total rewards and each individual's fairness.
